newsitem.title: FRANCE: French franc fall seen limited -economists.
newsitem.headline: French franc fall seen limited -economists.

text.p: The franc eased slightly against the mark on election projections showing France's Socialists-led opposition on course to victory after Sunday's parliamentary election runoff vote.

But economists took heart from the projections indicating the Socialists would be able to form a government without the Communists. "I'm not expecting the franc to weaken that much. I think people had a target of 3.40 per mark if the Socialists did not have an absolute majority," economist Philippe Brossard of ABN-Amro said. "The 3.3950 target is now out. It may test 3.3850 but will probably come back towards 3.37."
The franc was trading at 3.3822 per mark at 1840 GMT compared with 3.3816 late on Friday.
The likelihood that the Communists would not be included in any Socialist-led government "is the silver lining" to the results, said Marie Owens-Thomsen of Dresdner Kleinwort Benson.
"For the franc, even in the worst case scenario, I still do not see it falling lower below 3.40 per mark if the Socialists can form a government."

Owens-Thomsen said election of the Socialists, who advocate a more flexible position on meeting conditions for European monetary union, could damage prospects for a single currency but added "I feel the biggest risk now is from Germany."
Michala Marcussen, economist at Societe Generale, also said that, barring anything unforseen, 3.40 per mark appeared to be as low as the franc would go.
"There could be periods of weakness for the franc but I do not see it going beyond 3.40 per mark," she said.
Another economist, who did not wish to be named, said the fact the Socialists were committed to monetary union was protecting the currency.
"As far as European policy, nothing has changed," he said. "They may want to make some minor changes to economic policy, but they do not want to endanger the European project," he said.
"Also the Bank of France is independent. If the new government does something really extreme, the Bank will be there to sanction the government and to hike interest rates," he added.

The franc stayed relatively stable throughout the election campaign. It was trading at 3.3762 per mark on April 21, the day President Jacques Chirac announced the snap vote to give him a free hand in the runup to monetary union.
It started falling against the mark on April 17 from near a four-year high of 3.3621 when talk of a snap election first surfaced.
The lowest it traded at during the campaign was 3.3828 on May 28. That was its weakest level since February 4, when it fell to 3.3839 per mark.
